title: Yang Kyoungjong — the man who fought for three armies (or a legend?)
sources: Wikipedia: Yang Kyoungjong — 'purported' to have served in the Imperial Japanese Army, the Soviet Red Army and the German Wehrmacht; his existence and personal history are not substantiated by the historical record. Antony Beevor and Steven Zaloga present him as fact but give no sources. Zaloga's unsourced account: conscripted into Japan's Kwantung Army (Korea was then ruled by Japan), captured by the Soviets at Khalkhin Gol, sent to a Gulag labour camp and then the Eastern Front, captured by the Germans in 1943 near Kharkov and put into the 'Eastern Battalions'. Beevor: sent to Normandy with a battalion of former Soviet prisoners, captured by US paratroopers in June 1944. A photo taken after D-Day shows an unidentified man in Wehrmacht uniform; the official caption calls him a 'young Japanese'; the identity has never been verified. Stephen Ambrose recorded US officer Robert Brewer's account of capturing four Koreans in Wehrmacht uniforms who had been conscripted by Japan, captured by the Red Army and then by the Wehrmacht. A 2005 Korean SBS documentary found no convincing evidence of Yang's existence; historian Martin Morgan believes the man in the photo was a Georgian from the 795th Georgian Battalion.

Photos (public domain / CC0, Wikimedia Commons / US National Archives / Imperial War Museum / Polish National Digital Archive): the unidentified Asian prisoner in German uniform, Normandy, June 1944; the Kwantung Army in Mongolia, 1939; Khalkhin Gol, 1939; Eastern volunteers in German service; Utah Beach; German prisoners in Normandy

Archive film (public domain): '1939. Khalkhin Gol' (Soviet documentary, timecode cropped); 'Why We Fight: The Battle of Russia' (US War Department, 1943); 'D-Day 1944' (United News / Office of War Information) — all illustrative
Music: Arirang — US Army, public domain

post.facebook:
He fought for Japan, then for the Soviet Union, then for Nazi Germany. And the Americans captured him on D-Day.

At least, that's the legend of Yang Kyoungjong. A young Korean — Korea was then a Japanese colony — is drafted into the Japanese army. In 1939, on the Mongolian border, the Soviets capture him and send him to a labour camp. When Hitler invades, the Red Army hands him a rifle. In 1943, near Kharkov, the Germans capture him and put him in a German uniform, with a battalion of former Soviet prisoners, and send him to guard Normandy. On D-Day, American paratroopers capture Asian men in German uniforms that nobody can understand.

And there's the famous photo: an unidentified prisoner in Normandy, captioned by the US Army as a "young Japanese".

But famous historians who told the story as fact gave no source. A 2005 Korean documentary found no proof Yang ever existed, and one historian believes the man in the photo was from Georgia. Yet a US officer, Robert Brewer, did report capturing four Koreans in German uniforms who had fought for Japan and Russia first.

Real man — or did the war invent him? 👇

He fought for Japan, then for the Soviet Union, then for Nazi Germany — and the Americans captured him on D-Day. At least, that's the legend of Yang Kyoungjong.

Historians like Beevor and Zaloga told the story as fact, but without sources; the famous photo of an Asian prisoner in German uniform in Normandy was never identified, a 2005 Korean documentary found no proof he existed, and one historian thinks the man was Georgian. Yet a US officer did report capturing four Koreans in German uniforms who had fought for Japan and Russia first. Real man or legend?
